title: Best Digital Wardrobe Apps (2026): 10 Closet Apps Compared
h1: The best digital wardrobe apps in 2026: closet apps and outfit planners compared
excerpt: The best digital wardrobe apps of 2026 compared: free picks, Android and iPhone options, AI outfit planners, prices and privacy, from official listings.
tldr: The best digital wardrobe app depends on your phone and how much help you want. Indyx and Alta have the most generous free offers, Stylebook is a one-off purchase for iPhone, and Alta, GetWardrobe, Acloset and Fits suggest outfits with AI. Test any app with your 20 to 30 most-worn pieces before paying.
body:
The best digital wardrobe app for most people is a free one that runs on the phone they already use. Indyx (free, no item limit) and Whering (free, with paid extras) cover iPhone and Android, Stylebook is a one-off purchase for iPhone and iPad, and Alta, GetWardrobe, Acloset and Fits suggest outfits with AI. Indyx also sells sessions with human stylists.

This list of the best wardrobe apps, also sold as digital closet, virtual closet or outfit planner apps, covers what ten of them do, what they cost and who they suit. It uses each app's official website and its App Store and Google Play listings, checked in October 2026; we haven't tested the apps ourselves. Prices come from US listings and vary by country, and features change, so check the listing before you pay.

FitWardrobe is our app, and it isn't available yet, so it isn't ranked or in the table. There's a short note on it after the list.

Quick picks: the best digital wardrobe app for each need

  • Free: Indyx, with unlimited items, outfits and calendar entries on its free tier. Alta lists no paid plan at all.
  • Android: Acloset (a Google Play Editors' Choice in the US), Whering or Fits. Stylebook has no Android version.
  • iPhone, paid once: Stylebook, a one-time $4.99 in the US.
  • AI outfit suggestions: Alta for free; GetWardrobe or Acloset if a 100-item free tier or a subscription suits you.
  • Privacy: Stylebook, which keeps your data on your device (and in iCloud if you choose) and describes no account system.
  • Human stylists: Indyx, with virtual sessions listed from $60.
  • Outfit planning: Stylebook, Fits or GetWardrobe, which all have an outfit calendar.
  • On a computer: GetWardrobe (Mac and web app), or Whering and Alta in a browser.
  • Capsule wardrobes: Cladwell, which builds capsules and can add clothes without photos.
  • Nothing to photograph: Google Photos Wardrobe, for eligible users in the US, Brazil and India.

Free limits and prices change without much notice, so check the listing on the day you sign up.

The 10 best wardrobe apps, one by one

The order isn't a score. It runs roughly from general-purpose closets to more specialised tools.

1. Whering

Best for: a free closet with lots of ways to add clothes.

Whering lets you add pieces from a database of more than 100 million items, from retailer websites or from your own photos with the background removed, and there's a Chrome extension too. Dress Me shuffles outfits from your closet, and there's an event planner, packing lists and stats such as cost per wear. An October 2026 iPhone update says the planner now suggests outfits from your wardrobe and the weather. Friends' closets, moodboards and wishlists add a social side.

Price: free to use. The Outfit Maker is a paid extra, listed as a $4.99 in-app purchase on the US App Store in October 2026.

Worth knowing: there's no iPad version, and the Google Play data safety section says the app may share photos and videos with third parties.

2. Indyx

Best for: a free closet with no item limit, plus optional human stylists.

Indyx removes photo backgrounds automatically, imports pieces from forwarded receipts or product links, and uses AI to tag category, subcategory and colour. You build outfits on drag-and-drop boards, plan them on a calendar and get cost per wear worked out for you; Collections handle capsules and packing lists. It doesn't generate outfits with AI. Its listing promises "No random outfits styled by robots" and points to human stylists instead.

Price: the free tier includes unlimited items, outfits and calendar entries. Indyx Insider was listed at $12.99 a month or $74.99 a year on the US App Store in October 2026, and stylist sessions start at $60.

Worth knowing: it's on iPhone, iPad and Android, with no web app mentioned. See our head-to-head of Whering, Indyx and Stylebook for a closer comparison.

3. Acloset

Best for: lots of AI features, for a small wardrobe or a subscription.

Acloset adds items from a photo or an online search and turns snapshots into shop-style images. Its listing describes an AI stylist chat, personal colour and fit analysis, daily outfits based on the weather and your schedule, an outfit calendar, cost per wear, trip packing and virtual try-on.

Price: its website says all features are free for up to 100 items, and the free version shows ads. The US App Store listed a Basic plan at $3.99 a month in October 2026, plus Premium and Expert tiers and credit packs.

Worth knowing: 100 items fills quickly once shoes, bags and coats go in. It carries an Editors' Choice badge on Google Play in the US.

4. Stylebook

Best for: iPhone users who want to pay once and style outfits themselves.

Stylebook is the manual option. You catalogue pieces with tags, season, colour, brand, fabric and size, remove backgrounds with AI, and build outfits on a free-form canvas or with Outfit Shuffle. A calendar logs or plans outfits, Style Stats shows your most and least worn pieces and cost per wear, and there are visual packing lists. It has no AI outfit suggestions.

Price: a one-time purchase, $4.99 in the US according to its FAQ.

Worth knowing: your data stays on your device, and in iCloud if you turn it on. It's iPhone and iPad only, with no Android plans "at the moment", and the last App Store update was in June 2025. On Android, try these Stylebook alternatives for Android.

5. Fits

Best for: unlimited items for free and a creative outfit builder.

Fits, from the German developer L. & J. Henne, lets you photograph clothes or clip them from the web, then build outfits by swiping or on a free canvas (its site compares it to Polyvore). There are mood boards, custom tags, a calendar with selfie logging and virtual try-on. Its AI stylist chat suggests outfits by style, weather and occasion and, since a September 2026 update, can suggest products. Friends can make outfits for you.

Price: free, including unlimited items and background removal. Fits Pro adds unlimited AI suggestions and AI tagging, and credit packs are extra.

Worth knowing: it's on iPhone, iPad and Android, with no web app. "Fits AI - Your AI Stylist" is a different app. For a Fits alternative, Whering (social and free) and Acloset (AI chat and try-on) cover similar ground.

6. GetWardrobe

Best for: planning outfits on a computer as well as your phone.

GetWardrobe syncs across Android, iPhone, iPad, Mac and a web app. AI detects category and colour and removes backgrounds, and you can import pieces from shops. Its AI Outfit Generator filters by weather, occasion and mood, and there's a collage maker, a calendar with the local forecast, capsules and cost-per-wear stats. Premium adds packing lists and family wardrobes.

Price: free for up to 100 items, counting clothes and outfits together, with a starter AI Outfit Generator (10 outfits per run). Premium was listed at $49.99 a year on its website in October 2026, in US dollars, and it says prices may vary by region.

Worth knowing: virtual try-on uses paid credits. Its site says it isn't a fashion social media app.

7. Alta

Best for: free AI outfit suggestions.

Alta (listed as Alta Daily) adds clothes from forwarded email receipts, its own database or your photos, and fills in details such as fabric and fit. It suggests outfits each day from the weather and your schedule, styles named events and builds outfits around a piece you choose. There's avatar try-on, an outfit log with cost per wear, and packing lists for multi-city trips.

Price: free. Its website says "Alta is free to use", and the US App Store listed no in-app purchases in October 2026.

Worth knowing: it includes shopping features, such as price-drop alerts and suggestions for gaps in your closet, and its App Store privacy label lists precise location, photos and search history as data linked to you. It runs on iPhone, iPad, Android and the web.

8. Cladwell

Best for: an AI chat stylist and capsules, without photographing everything.

Cladwell, now listed as "Cladwell: AI Stylist & Outfits", lets you add clothes by picking similar pieces from its catalogue, pasting a product link or taking a photo; its site says "Most people never take a single photo". You can chat with its AI stylist, get daily outfit ideas based on the weather and what you wear most, find your colour season and build capsule wardrobes. "See it on me" try-on needs a subscription.

Price: free to download with basic use; a subscription with a 7-day trial covers the rest, and AI features have usage limits. Its site and App Store description quoted different prices in October 2026, so check in the app.

Worth knowing: the Play link on Cladwell's own app page returned an error in October 2026, so use the working Google Play listing. Its FAQ says photos aren't used to train AI.

9. Pureple

Best for: iPhone users who want AI outfit feedback and try-on.

On iPhone, Pureple's listing describes auto-categorising, web import, AI style suggestions, "Instant Outfit Feedback by AI", try-on on a model, a calendar and trip packing. On Android, adding items and building outfits by hand are free with no limit, but the Style Me AI suggestions and calendar planning need Pureple Pro.

Price: free, with ads on Android. Pro is a weekly, monthly or yearly subscription, with the yearly plan listed at $89.99 in the US App Store description in October 2026.

Worth knowing: it was rated 2.5 from about 4,000 reviews on Google Play in October 2026, against 3.9 on the App Store, so read recent Android reviews first.

10. Google Photos Wardrobe

Best for: people in the US, Brazil or India who'd rather not photograph their clothes.

Google added a Wardrobe feature to Google Photos in 2026. It scans photos of you from the past four years, gathers the clothes it finds into a wardrobe you can filter by category, and lets you combine up to six items into an outfit and preview it on yourself.

Price and access: it's part of the free Google Photos app, but Google's help page says it's rolling out to Google AI Pro and Ultra subscribers "as well as other select users", and non-subscribers need "more than 1,000 photos of yourself". You also need to be in Brazil, India or the US with Face Groups turned on.

Worth knowing: it only knows clothes you've been photographed wearing, and saved outfits count toward your Google storage. It wasn't available in the UK, the EU, Canada or Australia as of October 2026.

Other names you'll see

Two more apps come up in other lists. Combyne is an outfit-making community built mostly on a shoppable catalogue of brands rather than your own clothes. Smart Closet by Rabbit Tech has an outfit builder, calendar and packing lists, but neither its Google Play nor its App Store listing had been updated in 2026 when checked in October.

Our app, FitWardrobe (not ranked)

FitWardrobe is our app, and it isn't available yet, which is why it isn't in the list. It's coming to Android and the web (iPhone users will be able to use the web version) and will be free during early access.

You photograph a piece and AI tags its type, colour, pattern, season and formality, which you can correct. Pick an occasion and you get an outfit built only from clothes you own, with a one-line reason it works and one or two alternatives, and the outfits you keep or skip shape later ones. You can also build an outfit around one piece. The wardrobe is stored on your device, but tagging sends a compressed photo to Google's Gemini API and suggestions send item details to Groq, so the AI features need an internet connection. It doesn't track wear, check the weather, make packing lists, keep a calendar or sync between devices.

How to choose the best wardrobe app for you

  1. Start with your devices. Stylebook is iPhone and iPad only, Whering has no iPad app, and Google Photos Wardrobe depends on where you live. To plan on a laptop, use GetWardrobe, Whering or Alta.
  2. Decide how you'll add clothes. Photographing everything is the biggest job. Receipt forwarding (Indyx, Alta), product databases (Whering, Cladwell) or your photo library (Google Photos) cut it down. Our guide on how to digitise your wardrobe covers the photos.
  3. Check the free limit. Acloset and GetWardrobe stop at 100 items, and WRAP's 2022 survey of more than 6,000 UK adults put the average wardrobe at 118 items of clothing.
  4. Choose suggestions or control. Alta, GetWardrobe, Acloset, Fits and Cladwell suggest outfits; Stylebook and Indyx are built for styling yourself. Our guide to free AI stylist apps and tools also covers chatbots.
  5. Read the privacy label. The App Store's App Privacy section and Google Play's Data safety section show what's collected and shared. Read about the privacy risks of wardrobe apps before uploading mirror selfies.
  6. Test before you pay. Add your 20 to 30 most-worn pieces and use the app for two weeks. Our look at whether wardrobe apps are worth it sets out a longer test.

If you searched for wardrobe management software for a business, such as a costume department or a uniform store, these apps won't fit: they're built for one person's clothes.

What wardrobe apps can't do

A wardrobe app only knows what you've added and what the photo shows. It can't tell that a jumper has started to pill or that a linen shirt creases by lunchtime.

  • Keep themselves current. Every purchase and donation has to be added or removed, or the suggestions drift away from what you own. Google Photos is a partial exception.
  • Judge fit. Virtual try-on shows roughly how an outfit looks, not how it fits, moves or feels.
  • Know your context. AI suggestions work from category, colour, occasion and sometimes the weather. They don't know your office's unwritten dress code, that you cycle to work or that you never wear yellow.
  • Hold their price. Free tiers change. Check what the free plan covers before you spend an evening adding 80 pieces.
  • Delete your account for you. Removing a cloud-based app from your phone leaves your account and photos on the company's servers. Use the in-app deletion option or the request process described on the store listing.

faq.q: What is the best free wardrobe app?
faq.a: Indyx and Alta had the most generous free offers on their official listings in October 2026. Indyx's free tier includes unlimited items, outfits and calendar entries, and Alta lists no paid plan at all. Whering and Fits are also free to start, with paid extras, while Acloset and GetWardrobe are free only up to 100 items. Free limits change, so check the current listing.

faq.q: Is there an app for putting together outfits?
faq.a: Yes. Most digital wardrobe apps let you photograph your clothes and combine them into outfits on screen. Some, such as Alta, GetWardrobe, Acloset, Fits and Cladwell, suggest complete outfits with AI, often using the weather or an occasion. Others, such as Stylebook and Indyx, give you a canvas to build outfits yourself and a calendar to plan them.

faq.q: What is the best wardrobe app for Android?
faq.a: Acloset, Whering, Fits, Indyx and GetWardrobe all have Android apps with a free starting tier, and Acloset carried a Google Play Editors' Choice badge in the US in October 2026. Stylebook has no Android version, and Pureple's Android app keeps its AI suggestions for paying users. Google Photos Wardrobe needs Android 10 or later and works only in the US, Brazil and India.

faq.q: Is there a digital wardrobe app I can use on a computer?
faq.a: Yes. GetWardrobe syncs between your phone, a Mac and a web app, so you can plan outfits on a laptop. Whering has a web sign-in and a Chrome extension for adding items from shops, and Alta can be used on the web on a laptop. Stylebook doesn't run on computers, and Indyx and Fits don't mention a web version on their listings.

faq.q: What is the best capsule wardrobe app?
faq.a: Cladwell puts capsules at the centre: its listing includes capsule wardrobes alongside an AI chat stylist, with a subscription for the fuller features. Indyx lets you group pieces into Collections for a capsule or a trip, and GetWardrobe has a capsules feature. Any app with tags and outfit planning works if you'd rather choose the pieces yourself.

faq.q: Are wardrobe apps safe to use?
faq.a: It depends on the app, because they hold personal data: photos of your clothes, sometimes your face and home, and what you buy. Read the App Privacy section on the App Store or Data safety on Google Play before signing up, crop out faces and backgrounds, and find the account deletion option. Apps that keep data on your device, such as Stylebook, share less.
